newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British Gas splits up, changes name.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British Gas splits up, changes name.

text.p: Shareholders in British Gas, one of the world's largest utilities, voted on Wednesday to break up the company through a demerger to fight increased competition in liberalised UK gas markets.

The demerger, which will take effect on Monday, sees the hiving off of the gas supply business in Britain, along with its Morecombe Bay gas fields off northwest England, into a new firm called Centrica.

The remaining British Gas rump, which will include the TransCo gas transportation and storage business and the group's exploration and production and other international businesses, is to be renamed BG Plc.

"We believe that we should take the initiative in separating the competitive trading business from the monopoly transportation system, rather than wait until we are forced to do so (by industry regulator Ofgas)," chairman Richard Giordano told shareholders at a special meeting.
Shareholders overwhelmingly voted in favour of the demerger, which should see greater management focus and improved service.
"One of the major reasons for the demerger is to improve service to our customers," British Gas chairman Richard Giordano told shareholders.
British Gas was swamped last year by customer complaints over faulty bills due to problems with new computer software.
The group, which originated in the late 1940s and was privatised in 1986, first announced its split-up plan a year ago after witnessing whirlwind changes to its business environment.

Its monopoly in the market for industrial users, roughly half of the total British natural gas market, was the first to be dismantled in 1991 and British Gas consequently saw its share of this market drop to below 35 percent last year.
Competition is now being extended to the domestic, household market, which should be wholly opened up by 1998.
Increased competition has left British Gas struggling with the so-called "take-or-pay" contracts, mostly signed before privatisation.
These long-term deals with North Sea gas producers oblige British Gas to buy fixed amounts of gas at set prices, which are often higher than levels in the spot market.

But as competitors moved in, British Gas has been left with more gas than it can sell on. Several contracts have been renegotiated and Centrica will continue to try to strike more settlements this year.
"We still have a volume problem and a significant price problem. So we have to do more deals," Centrica's chief executive Roy Gardner told reporters after the shareholders' meeting.

Centrica has been regarded by market watchers as a takeover target for firms who want to expand in the British gas and electricity markets. Centrica shares traded up five pence at 75-1/2 on Wednesday in the grey market, on a when-issued basis.
But Giordano, who will continue to be chairman for both BG and Centrica, said no merger talks were being held with any party. "We are not talking to anybody about anything," he said.

Meanwhile, BG Plc -- now protected from the take-or-pay burden -- is awaiting the outcome of an inquiry by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) into a tough pricing policy for its TransCo unit proposed by industry regulator Ofgas.
The proposals would seriously dent BG's profits if the MMC fully accepts them. The MMC is due to report in April at the earliest. British Gas shares were down 4-1/4 in the grey market at 163.

BG's chief executive, David Varney, said the company was assessing its gas field portfolio. A newspaper report recently said the company had decided to sell certain non-core assets, but Varney told reporters this was speculation.
